newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SA WEEK AHEAD - FEB RESERVES SEEN OVER 12 BLN RAND.
newsitem.headline: SA WEEK AHEAD - FEB RESERVES SEEN OVER 12 BLN RAND.

text.p: The continuing flood of capital inflows into South Africa is expected to have swept reserves over half-a-billion rand higher in February, economists said.
If expectations are met, the figure will provide some respite to local financial markets which were besieged by a welter of mainly disappointing indicators last Thursday.
According to a Reuters consensus poll of 10 economists, gross reserves are expected to climb to 12.4 billion rand in February from 11.76 billion rand in January -- the highest level since March 1996.
The average was drawn from a range of 10.8 billion to 13.4 billion rand.
Most analysts put the rise down to increased foreign inflows but one said the figure would be boosted by offshore borrowing by the central bank.
The Reserve Bank will release February gold and foreign exchange reserves data at 1600 GMT on Friday.
Deutsche Morgan Grenfell economist Gordon Smith said the key issue in the February data would be the extent to which capital inflows would be offset by debt repayments during the month.
South Africa repayed 1.4 billion rand of an Ecu loan and around 500 million rand of the country's renegotiated standstill debt during the month.
This would have been countered, however, by foreign capital inflows into local gilt and equity markets, which economists estimate amounted to around 2.4 billion rand.
"Offshore banks offloaded a lot of dollars at the beginning of the month and then didn't do much in the second part of the month," ING Barings economist Hania Farhan said.
SMK Securities economist Herman van Papendorp said a good indication of the extent of inflows in the month could be gleaned from the rand's performance against the dollar.
He said the average rand/dollar exchange rate so far this month was around 4.45 from 4.64 in January, and it had firmed to 4.47 by the end of February from 4.57 at the end of January.
"The stronger rand would have also reduced the need for the Reserve Bank to intervene in the currency market," Farhan noted.

BOE NatWest chief economist Nick Barnardt was more circumspect in his forecast, pointing to the fact that the money market shortage had been unseasonally high during the month, suggesting there may have been a slight outflow of capital.
The shortage remained steady around the 10 billion rand level throughout February.

One economist who asked not to be identified said the rand's weakness in the latter half of the month indicated there had been a fair amount of capital outflows during the month, which he said had led to the central bank borrowing offshore.
"If they didn't borrow offshore during the month, the reserves would not have risen," he said, adding that he expected a 600 million rand increase in gross reserves.
The gold component of the equation was expected to derive little benefit from bullion's revival late this week.

Gold pushed through the $360 level late this week -- its highest level since the beginning of the year -- largely on the back of a stronger platinum price, which fixed at a six-month high of $398.75 on Friday morning

But most economists expected the gold valuation in the reserves to be lower than 1,441 rand per ounce registered in January, although this would be more than offset by the heavy portfolio flows seen during the month.
